title: Hands-on Exercise 01B
text:
R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics - 2  Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R


In general, thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices, just to mention a few of them.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyze, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()

Draw a cartographic standard choropleth map

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`

qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")











Despite its usefulness of drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the disadvantge of qtm() is that it makes aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. To draw a high quality cartographic choropleth map as shown in the figure below, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))

[plot mode] fit legend/component: Some legend items or map compoments do not
fit well, and are therefore rescaled.
ℹ Set the tmap option `component.autoscale = FALSE` to disable rescaling.











tm_shape() is used to define the input data (i.e mpsz_pop2024) and tm_polygons() is used to draw the planning subzone polygons

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()














Note



By default, it plots areas of polygons in light gray (gray85) and polygons borders in slightly dark gray (gray25).





To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we just need to assign the target variable such as Dependency to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")











Draws a choropleth map by using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Add the boundary of the planning subzones using tm_borders()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Notice that light-gray border lines have been added on the choropleth map.
The fill_alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).
Beside fill_alpha argument, there are three other arguments for tm_borders(), they are:

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.


tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")














Quantile data classification that used 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Using equal data classification method:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

  tm_polygons()














Note



By default, it plots areas of polygons in light gray (gray85) and polygons borders in slightly dark gray (gray25).





To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we just need to assign the target variable such as Dependency to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")











Draws a choropleth map by using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Add the boundary of the planning subzones using tm_borders()

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Notice that light-gray border lines have been added on the choropleth map.
The fill_alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).
Beside fill_alpha argument, there are three other arguments for tm_borders(), they are:

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.


tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")














Quantile data classification that used 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Using equal data classification method:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on the both sides of the existing cycling path. You are tasked to determine the extend of the land need to be acquired and their total area.



Firstly, st_buffer() of sf package is used to compute the 5-meter buffers around cycling paths.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(   cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)

This is followed by calculating the area of the buffers as shown in the code chunk below.

buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)

In this section, you will learn how to project a simple feature data frame from one coordinate system to another coordinate system. The technical term of this process is called projection transformation.


This is an example the coordinate system of mpsz simple feature data frame by using st_crs() of sf package as shown in the code chunk below.

title: Hands-on Exercise 02
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis is the evaluation of the pattern, or distribution, of a set of points on a surface. It can refer to the actual spatial or temporal location of these points or also include data from point sources. It is one of the most fundamental concepts in geography and spatial analysis.
This exercise has 2 parts:
Part1 covers First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which focus on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
Part2 cover Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which examine the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.






Notereferences



r4gdsa chap 04 - First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
r4gdsa chap 05 - Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods





In this part, spatstat is used to perform commonly used 1st-PPA methods in order to answer the specific questions:

Are the children centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
If the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

Clark-Even Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis Method & Kernel Density Estimation Method will be used to answer the above questions.


To provide answers to the questions above, two data sets will be used. They are:

Child Care Services data from data.gov.sg, a point feature data providing both location and attribute information of childcare centres.
Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data.

Working with different kernel methods






TipKernel methods used in density.ppp()



In spatstat, the kernel smoothing function (passed via the kernel argument in density.ppp()) defines the weighting shape used to spread each point’s mass across the surface.
Available Kernel Methods

"gaussian" (Default): A bell-shaped normal distribution curve. It produces the smoothest surface and extends infinitely (truncated computationally), making it the standard choice for most point pattern analyses.
"epanechnikov": A inverted parabolic kernel (\(1 - r^2\)). It is mathematically optimal in minimizing asymptotic mean integrated squared error (MISE) and has bounded, finite support.
"quartic" (or Biweight): A smooth, bell-like polynomial function with finite support (\((1 - r^2)^2\)). It drops off more steeply at the boundaries than Gaussian while remaining smoother than Epanechnikov.
"disc": A flat, uniform cylindrical kernel where all points within the bandwidth radius receive equal weight, resulting in sharp, step-like density transitions.

Second-order spatial point pattern analysis examines the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.
In this part, appropriate functions of spatstat are used to discover the spatial point processes of childcare centres in Singapore to answer the specific questions:

are the children centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
if the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?







Noterefereces



Methods used for second-order spatial point pattern analysis








Method / Function
Purpose
Interpretation relative to CSR


G-Function


Gest()
Measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest event.
• Above CSR: Clustering


• Below CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


F-Function


Fest()
Measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary point in space to the nearest observed event (empty space function).
• Below CSR: Clustering (larger empty spaces)


• Above CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


K-Function


Kest()
Evaluates the expected number of events within distance \(r\) of a typical event, normalized by intensity.
• Above CSR: Clustering at scale \(r\)


• Below CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


L-Function


Lest()
Linearized, variance-stabilized transformation of Ripley’s K-function, typically plotted as \(L(r) - r\).
• \(L(r) - r > 0\): Clustering


• \(L(r) - r < 0\): Regularity / Dispersion


• \(L(r) - r = 0\): Complete Spatial Randomness


Monte Carlo Envelopes


envelope()
Generates simulation envelopes (critical bands) under CSR to statistically test null hypotheses (\(H_0\)).
• Outside Envelope: Significant departure from CSR (\(p < \alpha\))


• Inside Envelope: Cannot reject CSR

The Clark-Evans test is a distance-based statistical method used in Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) to determine whether a spatial point pattern exhibits clustering, regularity (dispersion), or Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).
Key Concept & Aggregation Index (\(R\))
The test compares the mean observed nearest neighbor distance (\(\bar{r}_O\)) to the expected mean distance under CSR (\(\bar{r}_E\)):
$$R = \frac{\bar{r}_O}{\bar{r}_E}$$

\(R = 1\): The pattern is randomly distributed (consistent with CSR).
\(R < 1\): Observed points are closer together than expected \(\rightarrow\) Clustered pattern.
\(R > 1\): Observed points are farther apart than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regular / Dispersed pattern (\(R \approx 2.15\) indicates a perfectly hexagonal lattice).

Hypothesis Testing

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The point events are randomly distributed across the study region.
Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): The point events are not randomly distributed (or specifically clustered: \(R < 1\), or regular: \(R > 1\)).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
In R, the test is performed using clarkevans.test() from the spatstat.explore package.

Standard Z-Test:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                  correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered") 
Monte Carlo Simulation Test:
Compares the observed \(R\) value against simulated realizations of CSR to derive an exact empirical \(p\)-value:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                     correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered",                  
method = "MonteCarlo",                  
nsim = 999) 




Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a fundamental first-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis (1st-SPPA) technique used within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA). It transforms discrete, observed point events into a continuous density surface, revealing spatial hotspots and variations in event intensity without imposing strict parametric assumptions.
Core Mechanics in spatstat

Basic Function: Computed using density() on a planar point pattern (ppp) object.
Pixel Image Output: The resulting object belongs to class im, representing a 2D regular pixel array where each cell contains the estimated point density.
Unit Rescaling: Because default projected coordinates (such as SVY21 in meters) produce very small numbers (points per \(\text{m}^2\)), rescale.ppp() is commonly applied to convert units to kilometers (points per \(\text{km}^2\)) for clearer interpretation.

Key Tuning Parameters & Methods

Bandwidth (\(\sigma\)) Selection: Controls the degree of smoothing.



bw.diggle(): Optimal for detecting isolated, tight clusters amidst random noise.
bw.ppl(): Recommended when the point pattern predominantly consists of tight clusters.
bw.CvL() & bw.scott(): Alternative cross-validation and rule-of-thumb bandwidth estimators.

Kernel Smoothing Types: Defines the weighting function around each point (gaussian by default, epanechnikov, quartic, or disc).
Edge Correction: Setting edge = TRUE adjusts for intensity underestimation near the study boundary (window border).
Fixed vs. Adaptive Bandwidth:



Fixed (density()): Uses a uniform bandwidth \(\sigma\) across the entire region; sensitive to areas with extreme density variations (e.g., dense urban centers vs. sparse rural areas).
Adaptive (adaptive.density()): Dynamically adjusts the bandwidth based on local point concentration, applying smaller kernels in dense areas and wider kernels in sparse zones.


Cartographic Visualization Pipeline
To generate presentation-ready maps using packages like tmap:

Convert the spatstat im object to a raster using rast() from the terra package.
Assign the coordinate reference system (e.g., crs(kde_raster) <- "EPSG:3414").
Render continuous choropleth surfaces using tm_shape() + tm_raster().




K-Function is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that evaluates the spatial dependence (clustering, dispersion, or randomness) between point events across varying distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics (e.g., Clark-Evans or the G-function) which focus solely on the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points within a radius \(r\) around every typical point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} E[\text{number of extra points within distance } r \text{ of an arbitrary point}]$$

\(\lambda\) represents the mean point intensity across the study region.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the expected number of points within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), giving the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation of Results

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Pattern aligns with Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Kest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical K-Function:


R
# Estimate K with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic)
K_est <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_est, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Testing Complete Spatial Randomness (Monte Carlo Simulation):


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes 
K_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

If the observed curve lies above the upper envelope, clustering is statistically significant (\(p < \alpha\)).
If the curve lies below the lower envelope, dispersion/regularity is statistically significant.





The G-Function (Nearest Neighbor Distance Distribution Function) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest neighboring event.
Key Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the probability \(G(r)\) that an event’s nearest neighbor is located within a radial distance \(r\):
$$G(r) = P(d_i \le r)$$
Under the null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the theoretical distribution \(G_{theo}(r)\) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\) is:
$$G_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(G(r) > G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than expected at short distances, indicating that events are located closer to one another \(\rightarrow\) Clustering.
\(G(r) < G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than expected, indicating events maintain distance from one another \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(G(r) \approx G_{theo}(r)\): The point pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Estimation with Edge Correction:
Edge corrections (such as "border", "hanisch", or "best") adjust for unobserved points beyond the study boundary:


R
# Compute G-function estimation 
G_est <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical G(r) 
plot(G_est, xlim = c(0, 500)) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Uses envelope() to generate Monte Carlo simulation critical bands:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
G_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, correction = "all", nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed G(r) against simulation envelope 
plot(G_csr) 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The F-Function (also known as the Empty Space Function or point-to-event distance distribution) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary location in the study area to the nearest observed event.
Unlike the G-function (which measures distances between event pairs), the F-function samples the empty space across the entire study window.
Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the cumulative probability \(F(r)\) that an arbitrary point chosen at random within the observation window has at least one event within radial distance \(r\):
$$F(r) = P(d(x, Y) \le r)$$
where \(d(x, Y)\) is the shortest distance from an arbitrary point \(x\) to the nearest event in point pattern \(Y\).
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\), the theoretical baseline is:
$$F_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR
Because the F-function measures empty spaces:

\(F(r) < F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than CSR, meaning empty spaces are larger than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering (events group together, leaving wide gaps).
\(F(r) > F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than CSR, meaning points are evenly spread throughout the space \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(F(r) \approx F_{theo}(r)\): The pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Fest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical F-Function:


R
# Estimate F with edge correction (e.g., "best" or "raw") 
F_ck <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "best")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical F(r) 
plot(F_ck) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
F_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Fest, nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed F(r) against simulation envelopes 
plot(F_ck_csr) 

Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant clustering (\(p < \alpha\)).
Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion (\(p < \alpha\)).





The K-Function (Ripley’s K-Function) is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method used to evaluate whether point events exhibit clustering, dispersion, or randomness across multiple distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics, which only consider the distance to the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points found within a given radius \(r\) of any arbitrary point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbb{E}[\text{number of additional events within distance } r \text{ of a typical event}]$$

\(\lambda\) is the overall intensity of the point pattern.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process, the expected number of events within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), yielding the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected under randomness \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Follows Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Computing Empirical K-Function:
Estimated using Kest() with an edge-correction method (such as Ripley’s isotropic correction):


R
# Estimate K-function 
K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Evaluated using envelope() to run Monte Carlo simulations and establish critical confidence bands:


R
# Run Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The L-Function (Besag’s L-Function) is a variance-stabilized, linearized transformation of Ripley’s K-Function used in second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis.
While the K-function grows quadratically with distance (\(K(r) \approx \pi r^2\) under Complete Spatial Randomness), the L-function transforms this into a linear relationship, making departures from randomness easier to visually inspect and interpret across distance scales (\(r\)).
Mathematical Concept
Besag’s transformation scales the K-function as:
$$L(r) = \sqrt{\frac{K(r)}{\pi}}$$
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), \(K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2\), which simplifies to:
$$L_{theo}(r) = r \quad \iff \quad L(r) - r = 0$$
In practice, the L-function is almost always analyzed and plotted as the centered function \(L(r) - r\) (or \(L(d) - d\)) against distance \(r\).
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(L(r) - r > 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) exceeds CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r < 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) is less than CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r = 0\): Conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using Lest() and envelope() from spatstat:

Computing Empirical L-Function:


R
# Estimate L-function with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic) 
L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot centered L(r) - r against distance r 
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
L_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed L(r) - r against the simulation envelope 
plot(L_ck_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Inside Envelopes: No statistically significant departure from CSR.

Spatial Point Pattern Analysis is the evaluation of the pattern, or distribution, of a set of points on a surface. It can refer to the actual spatial or temporal location of these points or also include data from point sources. It is one of the most fundamental concepts in geography and spatial analysis.
This exercise has 2 parts:
Part1 covers First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which focus on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
Part2 cover Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which examine the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.

r4gdsa chap 04 - First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
r4gdsa chap 05 - Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods

Working with different kernel methods






TipKernel methods used in density.ppp()



In spatstat, the kernel smoothing function (passed via the kernel argument in density.ppp()) defines the weighting shape used to spread each point’s mass across the surface.
Available Kernel Methods

"gaussian" (Default): A bell-shaped normal distribution curve. It produces the smoothest surface and extends infinitely (truncated computationally), making it the standard choice for most point pattern analyses.
"epanechnikov": A inverted parabolic kernel (\(1 - r^2\)). It is mathematically optimal in minimizing asymptotic mean integrated squared error (MISE) and has bounded, finite support.
"quartic" (or Biweight): A smooth, bell-like polynomial function with finite support (\((1 - r^2)^2\)). It drops off more steeply at the boundaries than Gaussian while remaining smoother than Epanechnikov.
"disc": A flat, uniform cylindrical kernel where all points within the bandwidth radius receive equal weight, resulting in sharp, step-like density transitions.

The Clark-Evans test is a distance-based statistical method used in Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) to determine whether a spatial point pattern exhibits clustering, regularity (dispersion), or Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).
Key Concept & Aggregation Index (\(R\))
The test compares the mean observed nearest neighbor distance (\(\bar{r}_O\)) to the expected mean distance under CSR (\(\bar{r}_E\)):
$$R = \frac{\bar{r}_O}{\bar{r}_E}$$

\(R = 1\): The pattern is randomly distributed (consistent with CSR).
\(R < 1\): Observed points are closer together than expected \(\rightarrow\) Clustered pattern.
\(R > 1\): Observed points are farther apart than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regular / Dispersed pattern (\(R \approx 2.15\) indicates a perfectly hexagonal lattice).

Hypothesis Testing

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The point events are randomly distributed across the study region.
Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): The point events are not randomly distributed (or specifically clustered: \(R < 1\), or regular: \(R > 1\)).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
In R, the test is performed using clarkevans.test() from the spatstat.explore package.

Standard Z-Test:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                  correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered") 
Monte Carlo Simulation Test:
Compares the observed \(R\) value against simulated realizations of CSR to derive an exact empirical \(p\)-value:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                     correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered",                  
method = "MonteCarlo",                  
nsim = 999) 




Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a fundamental first-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis (1st-SPPA) technique used within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA). It transforms discrete, observed point events into a continuous density surface, revealing spatial hotspots and variations in event intensity without imposing strict parametric assumptions.
Core Mechanics in spatstat

Basic Function: Computed using density() on a planar point pattern (ppp) object.
Pixel Image Output: The resulting object belongs to class im, representing a 2D regular pixel array where each cell contains the estimated point density.
Unit Rescaling: Because default projected coordinates (such as SVY21 in meters) produce very small numbers (points per \(\text{m}^2\)), rescale.ppp() is commonly applied to convert units to kilometers (points per \(\text{km}^2\)) for clearer interpretation.

Key Tuning Parameters & Methods

Bandwidth (\(\sigma\)) Selection: Controls the degree of smoothing.



bw.diggle(): Optimal for detecting isolated, tight clusters amidst random noise.
bw.ppl(): Recommended when the point pattern predominantly consists of tight clusters.
bw.CvL() & bw.scott(): Alternative cross-validation and rule-of-thumb bandwidth estimators.

Kernel Smoothing Types: Defines the weighting function around each point (gaussian by default, epanechnikov, quartic, or disc).
Edge Correction: Setting edge = TRUE adjusts for intensity underestimation near the study boundary (window border).
Fixed vs. Adaptive Bandwidth:



Fixed (density()): Uses a uniform bandwidth \(\sigma\) across the entire region; sensitive to areas with extreme density variations (e.g., dense urban centers vs. sparse rural areas).
Adaptive (adaptive.density()): Dynamically adjusts the bandwidth based on local point concentration, applying smaller kernels in dense areas and wider kernels in sparse zones.


Cartographic Visualization Pipeline
To generate presentation-ready maps using packages like tmap:

Convert the spatstat im object to a raster using rast() from the terra package.
Assign the coordinate reference system (e.g., crs(kde_raster) <- "EPSG:3414").
Render continuous choropleth surfaces using tm_shape() + tm_raster().




K-Function is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that evaluates the spatial dependence (clustering, dispersion, or randomness) between point events across varying distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics (e.g., Clark-Evans or the G-function) which focus solely on the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points within a radius \(r\) around every typical point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} E[\text{number of extra points within distance } r \text{ of an arbitrary point}]$$

\(\lambda\) represents the mean point intensity across the study region.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the expected number of points within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), giving the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation of Results

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Pattern aligns with Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Kest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical K-Function:


R
# Estimate K with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic)
K_est <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_est, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Testing Complete Spatial Randomness (Monte Carlo Simulation):


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes 
K_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

If the observed curve lies above the upper envelope, clustering is statistically significant (\(p < \alpha\)).
If the curve lies below the lower envelope, dispersion/regularity is statistically significant.





The G-Function (Nearest Neighbor Distance Distribution Function) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest neighboring event.
Key Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the probability \(G(r)\) that an event’s nearest neighbor is located within a radial distance \(r\):
$$G(r) = P(d_i \le r)$$
Under the null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the theoretical distribution \(G_{theo}(r)\) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\) is:
$$G_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(G(r) > G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than expected at short distances, indicating that events are located closer to one another \(\rightarrow\) Clustering.
\(G(r) < G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than expected, indicating events maintain distance from one another \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(G(r) \approx G_{theo}(r)\): The point pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Estimation with Edge Correction:
Edge corrections (such as "border", "hanisch", or "best") adjust for unobserved points beyond the study boundary:


R
# Compute G-function estimation 
G_est <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical G(r) 
plot(G_est, xlim = c(0, 500)) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Uses envelope() to generate Monte Carlo simulation critical bands:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
G_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, correction = "all", nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed G(r) against simulation envelope 
plot(G_csr) 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The F-Function (also known as the Empty Space Function or point-to-event distance distribution) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary location in the study area to the nearest observed event.
Unlike the G-function (which measures distances between event pairs), the F-function samples the empty space across the entire study window.
Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the cumulative probability \(F(r)\) that an arbitrary point chosen at random within the observation window has at least one event within radial distance \(r\):
$$F(r) = P(d(x, Y) \le r)$$
where \(d(x, Y)\) is the shortest distance from an arbitrary point \(x\) to the nearest event in point pattern \(Y\).
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\), the theoretical baseline is:
$$F_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR
Because the F-function measures empty spaces:

\(F(r) < F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than CSR, meaning empty spaces are larger than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering (events group together, leaving wide gaps).
\(F(r) > F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than CSR, meaning points are evenly spread throughout the space \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(F(r) \approx F_{theo}(r)\): The pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Fest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical F-Function:


R
# Estimate F with edge correction (e.g., "best" or "raw") 
F_ck <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "best")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical F(r) 
plot(F_ck) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
F_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Fest, nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed F(r) against simulation envelopes 
plot(F_ck_csr) 

Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant clustering (\(p < \alpha\)).
Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion (\(p < \alpha\)).





The K-Function (Ripley’s K-Function) is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method used to evaluate whether point events exhibit clustering, dispersion, or randomness across multiple distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics, which only consider the distance to the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points found within a given radius \(r\) of any arbitrary point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbb{E}[\text{number of additional events within distance } r \text{ of a typical event}]$$

\(\lambda\) is the overall intensity of the point pattern.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process, the expected number of events within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), yielding the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected under randomness \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Follows Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Computing Empirical K-Function:
Estimated using Kest() with an edge-correction method (such as Ripley’s isotropic correction):


R
# Estimate K-function 
K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Evaluated using envelope() to run Monte Carlo simulations and establish critical confidence bands:


R
# Run Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The L-Function (Besag’s L-Function) is a variance-stabilized, linearized transformation of Ripley’s K-Function used in second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis.
While the K-function grows quadratically with distance (\(K(r) \approx \pi r^2\) under Complete Spatial Randomness), the L-function transforms this into a linear relationship, making departures from randomness easier to visually inspect and interpret across distance scales (\(r\)).
Mathematical Concept
Besag’s transformation scales the K-function as:
$$L(r) = \sqrt{\frac{K(r)}{\pi}}$$
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), \(K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2\), which simplifies to:
$$L_{theo}(r) = r \quad \iff \quad L(r) - r = 0$$
In practice, the L-function is almost always analyzed and plotted as the centered function \(L(r) - r\) (or \(L(d) - d\)) against distance \(r\).
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(L(r) - r > 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) exceeds CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r < 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) is less than CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r = 0\): Conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using Lest() and envelope() from spatstat:

Computing Empirical L-Function:


R
# Estimate L-function with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic) 
L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot centered L(r) - r against distance r 
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
L_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed L(r) - r against the simulation envelope 
plot(L_ck_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Inside Envelopes: No statistically significant departure from CSR.

title: Hands-on Exercise 03
text:
Spatio-temporal point process (space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
This hands-on exercise used forest fires data to answer to answer the below questions: - are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent? - if the answer is NO, where and when the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?






Notereference



r4gdsa chap 06 - Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis.





The 2 data sets in national level downloaded from Indonesia websites: - modis_2024_Indonesia.csv, MODIS data is downloaded from Fire Information for Resource Management System. - The Indonesia nationwide ESRI shapefile is downloaded from Indonesia Geospatial portal. title: Hands-on Exercise 03
text:
Spatio-temporal point process (space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
This hands-on exercise used forest fires data to answer to answer the below questions: - are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent? - if the answer is NO, where and when the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?
